/Through Wednesday/...
Issued at 1120 PM MDT Wed Oct 21 2026

Widespread moisture remains over the state this evening, 
underneath a broad plume of moisture embedded in south-
southwesterly flow extending into Baja California and the east 
Pacific. While some light showers have occasionally made it into 
our forecast area today (including a couple sprinkles across the 
Denver metro!), the more significant precipitation remains over 
the southwestern half of the state, where significant rainfall is 
likely over the next 24-48 hours.

The main synoptic features will not change significantly on 
Thursday, leading to a largely similar forecast here. A broad 
ridge will remain centered over the southern Great Plains, while a
strong upper level low drifts from the southern California 
coastline towards the central CA/NV area by Thursday evening. The 
fetch of deep moisture will remain in place across the state, with
forecast specific humidity, integrated vapor transport, and 
precipitable water all reaching standardized anomalies of 4-6 
sigma... falling well outside the climatology for this time of 
year. Indeed, GJT's 00z sounding yielded a precipitable water of 
0.96" which shattered the daily record there. Of course, most of 
our forecast area is shielded by a few mountain ranges in this 
type of flow, meaning that we'll only see a few rounds of light to
moderate showers across the mountains on Thursday afternoon and 
evening when more organized convection can make it this far 
north/east. Across the plains... while soundings and ACARS data 
confirm there's plenty of moisture aloft (PW near 0.7-0.8" at 
DEN), the deep dry/mixed layer below ~650mb and surface dew point 
depressions close to 30F will keep things relatively quiet, 
outside of a couple weak showers during the afternoon. Very warm 
700mb temperatures - as warm as +8-10C - should lead to high 
temperatures in the 70s for the plains, with snow levels as high 
as 12-13kft over the mountains.

The main upper low should transition back to an open wave on 
Friday, as it begins to interact with a piece of a northern stream
trough/jet. The primary shortwave with this trough is expected to
track from southwestern Utah into western Wyoming, turning the 
flow a towards the southwest, leading to a gradual drying trend 
across the region. Mid-level flow does increase across the region,
but the stronger QG subsidence is off to our northwest and lee 
cyclogenesis will confine most of the stronger wind gusts to the 
southeast metro and plains (roughly along/south of I-76). In 
addition to the warm temperatures (highs in the upper 70s to near 
80F), there could be some spotty elevated/near critical fire 
weather conditions where lower RH overlaps with the gusty winds 
Friday afternoon.

The aforementioned interaction between the former cutoff low and 
the northern stream is where forecast uncertainty really begins to
grow, leading to a few different scenarios for the weekend/early 
next week. A second, weaker, cutoff low is expected to develop 
over the desert southwest by early Saturday. Meanwhile, a surface 
cold front should work through the lower elevations Saturday 
morning. We're confident that temperatures will be much cooler - 
with forecast highs somewhere in the 50s across the plains. As the
upper low drifts towards the Four Corners region, low/mid level 
moisture is expected to increase. At the very least, this should 
allow for widespread cloud cover to redevelop, with chances for 
precipitation increasing towards Saturday evening into Saturday 
night. Weak QG ascent combined with very weak/shallow upslope 
should be enough for scattered showers across most of the area, 
with guidance favoring the mountains south of I-70 and portions of
the far eastern plains (where isentropic lift is more prominent),
leaving most of the I-25 corridor in a relative minimum of QPF.

The upper low is expected to weaken as it lifts into northern 
Colorado by Sunday and Monday, though there is a rather large 
spread in both temperature and QPF forecasts across most of our 
forecast area in this period. Subtle differences in the 
strength/track of the 700/500mb lows will ultimately determine if 
we get another round of rain and snow late Sunday through Monday, 
or if we start to quickly dry out to start the week. A bi-modal 
distribution in QPF has been noted in some ensemble guidance 
today. Given that we're still 4-5 days out, I would expect it'll 
take at least a couple days before we can feel confident about the
timing or precipitation amounts anywhere in our CWA. Either way, 
near/below normal temperatures are likely to continue Sunday and 
Monday.

While the overall forecast pattern remains murky, there is a 
fairly consistent signal for a modest warming/drying trend by mid-
week next week, with forecast high temperatures returning to near
or slightly above normal values.
